items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider an autonomous system written as
[MATH: \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),]
where [MATH: [x; y]] and [MATH: [f_{1}(x, y); f_{2}(x, y)]].

Content:
The system is called almost linear at an equilibrium point [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast] if the Jacobian determinant at this point is nonzero there, i.e.
[MATH: \det\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast)\bigr)\neq 0.]

Content:
For example, let
[MATH: [x + y + y^{2}; x + y]]

Content:
First, notice that [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},] so [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast] is an equilibrium.

Content:
Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

Content:
[MATH: (∂f_{1})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x + y + y^{2}) = 1,|(∂f_{1})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x + y + y^{2}) = 1 + 2y; (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x + y) = 1,|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x + y) = 1]
Thus, we have

Content:
[MATH: |1|1 + 2y; 1|1|]

Content:
Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium [MATH: [0; 0]] to get

Content:
[MATH: J(0, 0)|=|1|1 + 2(0); 1|1|; =|1|1; 1|1|; = 0.]

Content:
Finally, since the Jacobian is [MATH: 0,] the system is not almost linear at [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast].

items.title: Identifying Almost Linear Systems

sections.normalized_html:
Given the system of differential equations, determine whether the system is almost linear at the equilibrium point [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast= [0, \: 0]^T.]

[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = − y^{2}(t) + 1 − e^{x(t)}; y^{′}(t) = − x^{2}(t) + 1 − e^{y(t)}]
sections.readable_text:
Given the system of differential equations, determine whether the system is almost linear at the equilibrium point [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast= [0, \: 0]^T.]

[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = − y^{2}(t) + 1 − e^{x(t)}; y^{′}(t) = − x^{2}(t) + 1 − e^{y(t)}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as [MATH: \mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})] where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]] and [MATH: [− y^{2} + 1 − e^{x}; − x^{2} + 1 − e^{y}]]

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}).]

In our case, we have the following:

[MATH: |(∂f_{1})/(∂x)|(∂f_{1})/(∂y); (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)|]

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

[MATH: (∂f_{1})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(− y^{2} + 1 − e^{x}) = − e^{x},|(∂f_{1})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(− y^{2} + 1 − e^{x}) = − 2y; (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(− x^{2} + 1 − e^{y}) = − 2x,|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(− x^{2} + 1 − e^{y}) = − e^{y}]

Thus, we have

[MATH: |− e^{x}|− 2y; − 2x|− e^{y}|]

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium [MATH: [0; 0]] to get

[MATH: J(0, 0)|=|− e^{0}|− 2(0); − 2(0)|− e^{0}|; =|− 1|0; 0|− 1|; = (− 1)(− 1) − (0)(0); = 1; ≠ 0.]

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is [MATH: \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{almost linear}}] at [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose the system
[MATH: \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),]
is almost linear at an equilibrium [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast.] In this case, the system's behavior near [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast] can be approximated by a linear system.

Content:
First, we define the deviation from equilibrium by
[MATH: \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^\ast.]
Small values of [MATH: \mathbf{u}] correspond to points close to the equilibrium.

Content:
Next, assuming [MATH: \mathbf{x} = [x, y]^T,] we compute the Jacobian matrix
[MATH: [(∂f_{1})/(∂x)|(∂f_{1})/(∂y); (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)]]
and evaluate it at [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast] to obtain the constant matrix [MATH: J = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast).]

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},] the nonlinear system can be approximated by the linearized system
[MATH: \mathbf{u}'= J \mathbf{u}.]

Content:
This linear system captures the leading-order behavior of solutions close to the equilibrium.

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast=[2, \ 0]^T?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as [MATH: \mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})] where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]] and [MATH: [x^{2} + 3y − 4x + 4; x^{2} − 2x + y^{2}]]

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}).]

In our case, we have the following:

[MATH: [(∂f_{1})/(∂x)|(∂f_{1})/(∂y); (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)]]

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

[MATH: (∂f_{1})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} + 3y − 4x + 4) = 2x − 4,|(∂f_{1})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} + 3y − 4x + 4) = 3; (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} − 2x + y^{2}) = 2x − 2,|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} − 2x + y^{2}) = 2y]

Thus, we have

[MATH: [2x − 4|3; 2x − 2|2y]]

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium [MATH: [2; 0]] to get

[MATH: [2(2) − 4|3; 2(2) − 2|2(0)]]

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

[MATH: [0|3; 2|0]]

where the deviation vector is

[MATH: [x; y]]

[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = x^{2} + y^{2} − 5; y^{′}(t) = x^{2} − y^{2} − 3]
Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system’s solutions near the equilibrium [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast = \left[2,\ 1\right]^T?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as [MATH: \mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})] where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]] and [MATH: [x^{2} + y^{2} − 5; x^{2} − y^{2} − 3]]

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}).]

In our case, we have the following:

[MATH: [(∂f_{1})/(∂x)|(∂f_{1})/(∂y); (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)]]

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

[MATH: (∂f_{1})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} + y^{2} − 5) = 2x,|(∂f_{1})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} + y^{2} − 5) = 2y; (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} − y^{2} − 3) = 2x,|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} − y^{2} − 3) = − 2y]

Thus, we have:

[MATH: [2x|2y; 2x|− 2y]]

Now, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium [MATH: [2; 1]] to get

[MATH: [4|2; 4|− 2]]

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast.]

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation: [MATH: |4 − λ|2; 4|− 2 − λ||= 0; (4 − λ)(− 2 − λ) − (4)(2)|= 0; λ^{2} − 16|= 0]

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1 = -4, \quad \lambda_2 = 4.]

Finally, since we have two real eigenvalues with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an [MATH: \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable saddle}}.]

> The eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] of the Jacobian at the equilibrium are purely imaginary.

Content:
In this situation, the corresponding linearized system has a center at the origin, meaning that solutions neither grow nor decay, but instead circulate around the equilibrium.

Content:
For the original nonlinear system, however, this case is inconclusive. While the linearized system predicts closed orbits, the nonlinear system may exhibit a stable center, an unstable spiral, or other nearby behavior.

Content:
Therefore, when the Jacobian has purely imaginary eigenvalues, linearization alone is not sufficient to classify the equilibrium. In such cases, further analysis beyond linear approximation is required.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider an autonomous system written as
[MATH: \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),]
where [MATH: [x; y]] and [MATH: [f_{1}(x, y); f_{2}(x, y)]].

Content:
The system is called almost linear at an equilibrium point [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast] if the Jacobian determinant at this point is nonzero there, i.e.
[MATH: \det\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast)\bigr)\neq 0.]

Content:
For example, let
[MATH: [x + y + y^{2}; x + y]]

Content:
First, notice that [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},] so [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast] is an equilibrium.

Content:
Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

Content:
[MATH: (∂f_{1})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x + y + y^{2}) = 1,|(∂f_{1})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x + y + y^{2}) = 1 + 2y; (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x + y) = 1,|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x + y) = 1]
Thus, we have

Content:
[MATH: |1|1 + 2y; 1|1|]

Content:
Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium [MATH: [0; 0]] to get

Content:
[MATH: J(0, 0)|=|1|1 + 2(0); 1|1|; =|1|1; 1|1|; = 0.]

Content:
Finally, since the Jacobian is [MATH: 0,] the system is not almost linear at [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast].

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Almost Linear Systems

Example Prompt:
Given the system of differential equations, determine whether the system is almost linear at the equilibrium point [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast= [0, \: 0]^T.]

[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = − y^{2}(t) + 1 − e^{x(t)}; y^{′}(t) = − x^{2}(t) + 1 − e^{y(t)}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as
[MATH: \mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})]
where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]] and
[MATH: [− y^{2} + 1 − e^{x}; − x^{2} + 1 − e^{y}]]

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}).]

In our case, we have the following:

[MATH: |(∂f_{1})/(∂x)|(∂f_{1})/(∂y); (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)|]

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

[MATH: (∂f_{1})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(− y^{2} + 1 − e^{x}) = − e^{x},|(∂f_{1})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(− y^{2} + 1 − e^{x}) = − 2y; (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(− x^{2} + 1 − e^{y}) = − 2x,|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(− x^{2} + 1 − e^{y}) = − e^{y}]

Thus, we have

[MATH: |− e^{x}|− 2y; − 2x|− e^{y}|]

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium [MATH: [0; 0]] to get

[MATH: J(0, 0)|=|− e^{0}|− 2(0); − 2(0)|− e^{0}|; =|− 1|0; 0|− 1|; = (− 1)(− 1) − (0)(0); = 1; ≠ 0.]

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is [MATH: \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{almost linear}}] at [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Linear Approximations Near Equilibria

Content:
Suppose the system
[MATH: \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),]
is almost linear at an equilibrium [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast.] In this case, the system's behavior near [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast] can be approximated by a linear system.

Content:
First, we define the deviation from equilibrium by
[MATH: \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^\ast.]
Small values of [MATH: \mathbf{u}] correspond to points close to the equilibrium.

Content:
Next, assuming [MATH: \mathbf{x} = [x, y]^T,] we compute the Jacobian matrix
[MATH: [(∂f_{1})/(∂x)|(∂f_{1})/(∂y); (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)]]
and evaluate it at [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast] to obtain the constant matrix [MATH: J = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast).]

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},] the nonlinear system can be approximated by the linearized system
[MATH: \mathbf{u}'= J \mathbf{u}.]

Content:
This linear system captures the leading-order behavior of solutions close to the equilibrium.

Content:
Let's see an example.

---

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria

Example Prompt:
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = x^{2}(t) + 3y(t) − 4x(t) + 4; y^{′}(t) = x^{2}(t) − 2x(t) + y^{2}(t)]
Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point [MATH: \mathbf{x}^\ast=[2, \ 0]^T?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as
[MATH: \mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})]
where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]] and
[MATH: [x^{2} + 3y − 4x + 4; x^{2} − 2x + y^{2}]]

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}).]

In our case, we have the following:

[MATH: [(∂f_{1})/(∂x)|(∂f_{1})/(∂y); (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)]]

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

[MATH: (∂f_{1})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} + 3y − 4x + 4) = 2x − 4,|(∂f_{1})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} + 3y − 4x + 4) = 3; (∂f_{2})/(∂x)|= (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} − 2x + y^{2}) = 2x − 2,|(∂f_{2})/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} − 2x + y^{2}) = 2y]

Thus, we have

[MATH: [2x − 4|3; 2x − 2|2y]]

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium [MATH: [2; 0]] to get

[MATH: [2(2) − 4|3; 2(2) − 2|2(0)]]

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

[MATH: [0|3; 2|0]]

where the deviation vector is

[MATH: [x; y]]
